blog.title: Before your first site visit: a useful checklist
blog.excerpt: The drawings, questions and priorities that make an initial conversation more productive.
blog.content:
Start with your priorities
Write down how you want the property to work: rooms, circulation, privacy, storage and future needs. Separate essentials from preferences so the conversation has a clear starting point.

Bring what you have
Gather existing drawings, site photographs and available survey information. Make clear which documents are current and which still need verification. Do not assume a sketch is a construction drawing.

Discuss access and use
Explain whether the property will remain occupied, how materials could reach the site, and any practical restrictions. These details help identify questions for the next stage.

Leave with a written next step
Record who will provide missing information, what assessments are needed and what the next proposal will cover.

blog.title: What a clear construction scope should explain
blog.excerpt: Look beyond a headline figure to understand inclusions, exclusions and responsibilities.
blog.content:
Define the work
A useful scope identifies the spaces, work packages and intended deliverables. It should be possible to connect each item to a drawing, specification or agreed description.

Name the exclusions
Ask which items are outside the proposal: specialist design, utility connections, loose furniture or other work. The exact exclusions will depend on your project.

Record material choices
Document finish grades and approved samples. Where a selection is pending, agree how it will be priced and approved.

Agree a change process
A change should be described and approved before it affects the work. Record any impact on time and price in the project documentation.

blog.title: Making material and finish decisions with confidence
blog.excerpt: A practical way to compare appearance, maintenance and installation requirements.
blog.content:
Look at the real sample
A photograph may not show texture, variation or reflected light accurately. View a sample in the intended space where practical.

Ask about maintenance
Discuss cleaning requirements, exposure and the intended use of each finish with the supplier and designer. Different locations in the same building may need different specifications.

Coordinate details
Material thickness, edge treatments and junctions affect the final appearance. Resolve these details before ordering.

Record the selection
Keep the product reference, approved sample and quantity assumptions with the project specification. Confirm availability before finalising the programme.

faqs.question: How is a construction estimate prepared?
faqs.answer: An estimate starts with the site, usable area, drawings and a written specification. Ask for an itemised scope, exclusions and a process for approving changes before agreeing to a price.

faqs.question: What happens during a first site visit?
faqs.answer: A first visit is a chance to discuss access, existing conditions, intended use and available drawings. Bring your questions and site documents. Any surveys or professional assessments should be agreed separately.

faqs.question: How long will my project take?
faqs.answer: A programme depends on project size, design readiness, site access, procurement and weather. Request a project-specific schedule with milestones and a clear process for communicating delays.

faqs.question: Can I choose my materials and finishes?
faqs.answer: Record preferred materials and finish grades in the specification. Compare samples and agree any substitutions, price changes and lead-time impacts in writing.

faqs.question: Are design and approvals included?
faqs.answer: The written proposal should state which design, coordination and approval-support services are included. Confirm requirements with the relevant authority and qualified professionals for your particular site.

faqs.question: How are payments and changes handled?
faqs.answer: Agree documented milestones, payment stages and change-order approvals before work begins. The final contract, including warranties and exclusions, should reflect the actual project scope.
